newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

White sugar futures in London gave up earlier gains and closed mixed reflecting a lack of significant upward move in New York. December added $0.90 to close at $325, while other traded months were between $0.30 up to $0.90 a tonne down. In physicals, confusion was evident in the market over whether Sri Lanka had bought 12,500 tonnes of lesser-quality white sugar at its recent tender or decided to reinvite bids for later this week. In New York raw sugar futures backed off Wednesday's highs and closed mostly lower.

Heavy rains in Thailand reportedly caused some flood damage in the agricultural sector, although government sources said that the estimate for sugar cane production in 1996/97 (November/October) would remain unchanged at 62.42 million tonnes, up from 57.69 million tonnes produced the previous year. The higher tonnage is ascribed to expanded acreage in the northeast. Rapidly rising land prices are discouraging expansion in central Thailand. Otherwise, the market was devoid of fresh fundamental news.

GERMANY - Sugar production in August 1996 amounted to 1,960 tonnes, raw value, down from last year's 2,239 tonnes. This brought cumulative production in the first 11 months of 1995/96 (October/August) up to 4.15 million tonnes compared to 3.99 million tonnes in 1994/95. Total production in 1994/95 amounted to 3.99 million tonnes compared to 4.74 million tonnes in 1993/94. Sugar consumption in 1995/96 is also up. Total consumption in August 1996 reached 257,280 tonnes compared to 285,528 tonnes consumed in August 1995. This brought cumulative consumption in October/August 1995/96 up to 2.77 million tonnes against 2.74 million tonnes in 1994/95. Total consumption in 1994/95 amounted to 2.99 million tonnes against 2.94 million tonnes in 1993/94.

FRANCE - Sugar consumption in June 1996 amounted to 202,609 tonnes, raw value, down on last year's 219,364 tonnes. This brought cumulative consumption in the first nine months of 1995/96 up to 1.58 million tonnes compared to 1.60 million tonnes in the like period the previous year. Total consumption in 1994/95 amounted to 2.18 million tonnes against 2.21 million tonnes in 1993/94.

JAPAN - Sugar consumption continues to develop sluggishly. Total consumption in May 1996 reached 187,108 tonnes, down from last year's 191,939 tonnes. This brought cumulative consumption in the first eight months of 1995/96 (October/May) up to 1.77 million tonnes against 1.81 million tonnes in 1994/95. Total consumption in 1994/95 reached 2.62 million tonnes against 2.63 million tonnes in 1993/94.

UNITED STATES - Sugar imports under the 1995/96 (October/September) tariff rate quota up to September 29, 1996 amounted to 2,000,617 tonnes, raw value. This is equivalent to 92.19 per cent of the total quota of 2.17 million tonnes.

The European Union awarded 97,750 tonnes of white sugar at a maximum refund of ECU 45.064 per 100 kg at its weekly tender on Wednesday. Cumulative awards so far made under the 1996/97 series of tenders for the period up to October 2 reached 490 500 tonnes, which compares to 728 525 tonnes last year. Syria bought 13,000 tonnes of raw sugar from a European trade house at $312.94 per tonne and 13,000 tonnes of white sugar from a London-based house at $364 a tonne. Both cargoes are for November shipment. Jordan bought 30,000 tonnes of white sugar in two lots for shipments starting in mid-November. One lot of 15,000 tonnes is for shipment in the second half of November and was bought at a price of $367.00 per tonne, c&f. The rest is for shipment in the first half of December and was bought at $360.50, c&f. The sugar was bought from Paris-based Louis Dreyfus. Tunisia bought one cargo of white sugar for shipment in June, 1997 at $356.50 per tonne, c&f. Confusion surrounded at the result of Sri Lanka's sugar tender in the London market on October 3. Traders were unclear whether Sri Lanka bought 12,500 tonnes of lesser-quality white sugar at its recent tender or had decided to reinvite bids for later this week.
